invalidated_assumptions.assumption_type: ERP biomarker specificity — N400 in MCI
invalidated_assumptions.prior_belief: Standard cognitive neuroscience expectation in MCI is that N400 amplitude — the neural correlate of semantic integration difficulty — is significantly altered during language processing, reflecting impaired lexical-semantic memory in amnestic MCI patients.
invalidated_assumptions.what_disproved_it: In P-362 (Yang & Huang 2023; single cohort 30 aMCI vs 30 controls, EEG), despite significantly worse behavioural metaphor accuracy (especially novel metaphors), ERP showed no significant group difference in N400 or LPC amplitude - contrary to the expected N400 alteration. Note: the metaphor 'rebound' effect masks the LPC (not the N400). This is a paradigm-specific, underpowered null rather than a general disproof.
invalidated_assumptions.clinical_implication: This may indicate N400-based aMCI screening could yield false-negatives, warranting evaluation of post-semantic-integration tasks; tentative given the small single-paradigm sample.
invalidated_assumptions.review_note: Human G5 2026-06-26: VALID. Paper explicitly calls null N400 contrary to expectation. Small N=30/30. | G5 CONFIRM-with-caveat 2026-07-29 (AI-adversarial): grounding verified vs summary; overclaim softened; scope/power caveat added.
invalidated_assumptions.g5_caveat: Single small (30 aMCI / 30 controls) cross-sectional study, one metaphor paradigm. The null N400 is underpowered and paradigm-specific ('not supported here', not proven absent). Rebound masks the LPC not the N400; the task-replacement implication is an extrapolation.
invalidated_assumptions.prior_audit_2026_08_29: ADD_NEW_PRIOR:KA-21. Set assumption_id=KA-21 as a weak supporter (strength 'weak'); fix the sample-size field to '60 - 30 aMCI/30 HC'. If the operator prefers strict disproof standards, demote to 'proposed' instead.

readjudication_2026_09_26.reader: assistant (a language model), under the operator's delegation of 2026-09-26: one auditor and one challenger instructed to refute it, each reading the source PDF and searching the corpus for the prior; the verdict was applied without a human re-reading, so it is not a gate
readjudication_2026_09_26.attestation: Partly attested, but not in the form the record gives it. P-28 (EEG early-diagnosis review, Int J Psychophysiol 2022; PDF downloads/4. Computational Models and Modern AI Architectures/1-s2.0-S0167876022002471-main.pdf): 'N400 might be a promising biomarker of AD, since the deficits of lexical and semantic processing are the significant feature of AD (Venneri et al., 2018). Indeed, the latency of N400 delayed in normal aging (Federmeier and Kutas, 2005), AD (Taylor and Olichney, 2007), and MCI (Olichney et al., 2002). On the other hand, N400 amplitude in AD has been reported to be reduced in some studies (Grieder et al., 2013; Taylor and Olichney, 2007; Wolk et al., 2005), but also to be increased in others (Olichney et al., 2006; Taler et al., 2009).' P-370 (PDF 1-s2.0-S0010945221001507-main.pdf): 'altered N400 effects are associated with a higher risk of transiting to dementia in individuals with amnesic MCI (Olichney et al., 2008)'. So the corpus attests a delayed N400 latency in MCI and altered N400 repetition or congruity effects in amnestic MCI converters, and it reports N400 amplitude findings as mixed in direction even in AD. No corpus study states the record's 'standard expectation' that N400 amplitude is significantly altered in amnestic MCI. P-362 itself states only a hedged expectation that names no component: 'We assumed that the aMCI patients and normal control group might show some differences in the ERP data.' The assigned prior KA-21 (monotonic attenuation across SCD -> MCI -> AD) is not tested by P-362 at all: the study has two groups and no ordering of stages.
readjudication_2026_09_26.evidence: PDF: downloads/5. Neuroimaging and Neurophysiological Biomarkers/1-s2.0-S0001691823000707-main.pdf (Yang & Huang 2023, Acta Psychologica 235:103894). Design: 30 aMCI vs 30 NC, one metaphor sentence-final-word paradigm. Method: 'For each participant, ERPs were derived by averaging correctly classified trials on each type of target word', so the ERP contrast is conditioned on successful comprehension. N400 amplitude: 'We found a significant main effect of material type (F = 4.571, df = 58, p = 0.006), but the main effect of group (F = 2.729, df = 58, p = 0.104) and the interaction effect between group and material type (F = 1.213, df = 58, p = 0.312) was not significant.' N400 latency: 'group (F = 0.318, df = 59.35, p = 0.5749) [was] non-significant'. The direction matches attenuation: 'the NC group had a more negative N400 component than the aMCI group'; 'we found that the mean amplitude of N400 and LPC components of the aMCI group was lower than that of the NC group. However, the differences did not reach a statistically significant level.' Conclusion: 'ERPs showed that when accepted as meaningful, these sentences had similar waveforms to that of the NC group.' Limitations: 'although we expected to find between-group differences in the ERP components, no such differences were observed.' Behaviour (Table 3, NC vs MCI accuracy): conventional 87.75 vs 76.33, novel 57.42 vs 46.92, literal 94.25 vs 88.25, anomalous 92.58 vs 87.94. The group gap is largest for conventional metaphors (11.4 points against 10.5 for novel), so the record's 'especially novel metaphors' is not what the PDF shows: novel metaphors are simply the hardest condition in both groups. What this amounts to is a 30-vs-30 non-significant difference (p = 0.104) whose trend runs in the direction of the prior, measured on correct trials only in one paradigm. That is an underpowered null. It neither refutes nor bounds the belief, and the record itself concedes 'This is a paradigm-specific, underpowered null rather than a general disproof.'
readjudication_2026_09_26.audit_2026_08_29_assessment: Recommendation: 'ADD_NEW_PRIOR:KA-21. Set assumption_id=KA-21 as a weak supporter (strength weak); fix the sample-size field to 60 - 30 aMCI/30 HC. If the operator prefers strict disproof standards, demote to proposed instead.' The sample-size fix is right: the PDF has 30 aMCI + 30 NC = 60, and the P-362 block's '### What is the sample size?' says '30'. Linking the record to KA-21 is wrong, even as a weak supporter. KA-21 is a claim about ordering across stages (SCD -> MCI -> AD). P-362 compares two groups and orders no stages, and its non-significant trend (lower N400 and LPC amplitude in aMCI) points toward attenuation, not away from it. The fallback, demotion under strict disproof standards, is the correct choice under this round's rule that an underpowered null is not a disproof.
readjudication_2026_09_26.performance_flag: Not flagged. P-362 reports no discrimination metric: the registry has Best_Metric 'not reported', Validation V2, and the study reports ERP group statistics only. It is not in the Section 3.5 performance-validity list, so the demotion does not rest on the flag.
readjudication_2026_09_26.reasoning: The disproving evidence does not test the prior. P-362 is a 30-vs-30 study with one metaphor paradigm, and its ERPs are averaged over correctly judged trials only. The group effect on N400 amplitude is p = 0.104, with the aMCI amplitude lower, i.e. in the direction of the expected alteration, and N400 latency is null (p = 0.575). Under the round's rules an underpowered non-significant difference is not a disproof and not evidence of preserved function, and the record already calls it 'not a general disproof'. The prior as worded ('standard expectation ... N400 amplitude significantly altered ... in aMCI') is not stated in that form by any corpus study. The corpus (P-28, P-370) attests N400 latency delay and altered repetition or congruity effects in MCI, and P-28 records mixed directions for N400 amplitude even in AD. The KA-21 linkage is a category error, because P-362 orders no stages. Two secondary defects: the record says 'especially novel metaphors', which Table 3 contradicts, and the clinical implication ('N400-based aMCI screening could yield false-negatives') extrapolates from a null. The bibliographic anchor itself reconciles: the PDF is Yang & Huang 2023, DOI 10.1016/j.actpsy.2023.103894, matching the reference entry. Demote; the record does not survive as a cited invalidation. CHALLENGER CHECK (2026-09-26): re-read the P-362 extract. Every quoted statistic reconciles (group N400 amplitude F = 2.729, df = 58, p = 0.104; interaction p = 0.312; ERPs 'derived by averaging correctly classified trials'; the discussion attributes the lower aMCI amplitude to damage that 'had not formed significant difference with the healthy control group'). The behavioural group effect is real (chi2 = 22.435, p < 0.0001, NC > aMCI on all four materials), so the behaviour/ERP contrast is genuine, but the only expectation the paper states is its own hedged hypothesis ('the aMCI patients and normal control group might show some differences in the ERP data'; 'we expected to find between-group differences in the ERP components'), which is the study's hypothesis, not a field belief. The review_note's 'Paper explicitly calls null N400 contrary to expectation' refers to that own hypothesis. No attestation or evidence was missed that would rescue the record. Demote stands.

invalidated_assumptions.prior_belief: Population-level MCI prevention messaging consistently emphasises modifiable lifestyle factors — obesity (BMI), poor diet, and inadequate sleep — as primary risk drivers for cognitive decline. These are widely promoted as the most actionable targets for MCI prevention.
invalidated_assumptions.what_disproved_it: In a single cross-sectional Pune cohort (N=605, 40-60 yrs), BMI, diet type, and sleep duration were NOT associated with MCI in the fully adjusted model (p>0.05), whereas age, gender, education, severe stress, and low physical activity were (MCI prevalence 27.77%) - indicating a boundary condition for non-Western middle-aged populations rather than a disproof of lifestyle risk factors generally.
invalidated_assumptions.clinical_implication: In non-Western middle-aged adults, BMI/diet/sleep were not associated with MCI while stress and inactivity were - an association-level, cross-sectional boundary condition requiring longitudinal confirmation, not a field-level refutation of lifestyle-based prevention.
invalidated_assumptions.review_note: G5 moderate: BOUNDARY CONDITION for non-Western middle-aged populations (single cross-sectional Pune cohort N=605); not a field-level disproof of lifestyle risk factors. | G5 CONFIRM-with-caveat 2026-07-29 (AI-adversarial): grounding verified vs summary; overclaim softened; scope/power caveat added.
invalidated_assumptions.g5_caveat: Single cross-sectional single-city Pune cohort (N=605), self-reported lifestyle measures, clinical (not research) ACE-III cutoff. Shows absence-of-association in THIS non-Western population - a boundary condition, not a causal or field-level disproof.
invalidated_assumptions.prior_audit_2026_08_29: ADD_NEW_PRIOR:KA-22. Set assumption_id=KA-22 with strength 'weak/boundary-condition'; the same KA is anchored by IA-67 (P-249 meta-analysis). A single cross-sectional self-report null should not appear in Table 6.8 without that qualifier.

readjudication_2026_09_26.attestation: Attested only in a narrower form than the record states. P-266 itself (PDF downloads/1. Clinical Assessments, Behavioral and Social Factors/1-s2.0-S2213398423002774-main.pdf), Introduction: 'There are certain factors that influence the cognitive performance like age, gender, mid-life obesity, mid-life hypertension, sleep disturbances, lack of physical activity etc.'; Discussion 5.7: 'Studies suggests being overweight or obese in mid-life is a risk factor for dementia but in later life, being underweight is a risk factor.' P-797 block (verbatim quote of its paper): 'In 2020, The Lancet Commission on Dementia estimated that approximately 40 % of the global burden of dementia could be attributed to 12 modifiable risk factors: low education, traumatic brain injury, physical inactivity, obesity, diabetes, excessive alcohol consumption, hypertension, smoking, depression, hearing loss, social isolation, and air pollution [5].', after which sleep is introduced as outside that list ('two important and emerging factors linked to dementia'). P-635 block: 'Sleep disturbance is an emerging, potentially modifiable dementia risk factor'. So the corpus attests midlife obesity as a modifiable DEMENTIA risk factor, with sleep (and diet, P-745) as emerging candidates. Searched: summaries.md scanned for every sentence pairing 'risk factor'/'modifiable'/'attributable' with obesity/BMI/diet/sleep (136 hits read), plus the P-266 PDF. No corpus study states the record's form, that MCI prevention messaging 'consistently emphasises' BMI, diet and sleep as 'primary risk drivers' and 'the most actionable targets'. That wording was supplied by the reviewer, and diet and sleep are not on the Lancet list the corpus quotes. The linked prior KA-22 was registered by the 2026-08-29 audit from IA-29 and IA-67 themselves (status proposed_2026_08_29, currently_invalidated_by [IA-67, IA-29]). That is the circular registration Section 2 flags, not attestation.
readjudication_2026_09_26.evidence: P-266 PDF (downloads/1. Clinical Assessments, Behavioral and Social Factors/1-s2.0-S2213398423002774-main.pdf; Gazbare & Palekar 2024, doi 10.1016/j.cegh.2023.101490). The record's figures are accurate (N=605, 40-60 y, prevalence 27.77%; 'The other covariates such as marital status, family type, diet, BMI, sleep duration and lifestyle were not significantly associated with the MCI'), but the design does not test the prior. (1) It was powered for prevalence, not associations: 'the minimum required sample size calculated was 589'. (2) The outcome is a concurrent screening cut-off: 'We have considered ACE-III score of less than 88 as MCI' (the clinical cut-off; the paper gives 82 for research). A cross-sectional screen cannot test a belief about later dementia risk. (3) Diet is vegetarian vs non-vegetarian: 'Type of Diet: food type consumed for past 6 month were asked. Vegetarian- one who consumes only vegetables, non-vegetarian -one who eat meat, seafood and other animal product.' (4) Sleep is a self-reported dichotomy: 'people who sleeps for 6-8 h, 5 day/week was considered having adequate sleep'. (5) The nulls are imprecise (Table 3): 'BMI Normal 1 1.01 (0.60-1.68) 0.97 Overweight 1 1.11 (0.67-1.85) 0.66 Pre-obese 2 Reference'; 'Diet Veg 1 0.84 (0.54-1.32) 0.46'; 'Sleep duration Adequate 1 1.44 (0.94-2.19) 0.08'. (6) The authors do not read the nulls as a boundary: 'One of the reasons could be that the participants might have difficulty recalling their sleep duration.'; 'However, individuals with higher BMI showed less score on ACE-III indicating MCI.' (7) The paper makes no non-Western versus Western comparison. Low physical activity was associated with MCI (high vs low OR 0.33, 0.2-0.56), which is consistent with lifestyle messaging. Challenger addition (Methods 2.6.1 and Table 3): BMI was classified on WHO South Asian cut-offs ('underweight <=18.5, Normal 18.5 to 22.99, Overweight 23 to 24.99, Obese >=25'). Yet the analysed categories are only 'Normal', 'Overweight' and 'Pre-obese' (the reference group, n=181). Neither obesity nor underweight was contrasted, so the BMI null does not address the obesity leg of the prior. Authors' limitations: 'The study can fall into assessment bias, selection bias. Further studies utilizing longitudinal data ... could help'.
readjudication_2026_09_26.audit_2026_08_29_assessment: Recommendation: 'ADD_NEW_PRIOR:KA-22. Set assumption_id=KA-22 with strength weak/boundary-condition ... A single cross-sectional self-report null should not appear in Table 6.8 without that qualifier.' The reason is right: a single cross-sectional self-report null is weak evidence. The remedy is not. Registering KA-22 from this record is circular, and a 'weak' label cannot rescue a record whose evidence does not test its prior. P-266 fails all three terms of KA-22's own disproof_signal ('A well-powered trial or meta-analysis showing null or boundary-conditioned effects of the lifestyle factor on incident MCI/dementia'): it is not powered for associations, it is not a trial or meta-analysis, and its outcome is not incident MCI or dementia. The recommendation was never applied (strength is still 'moderate'), and demotion supersedes it. The record's gate was a delegated model pass ('G5: AI-adversarial verification (Opus), operator-delegated 2026-07-29'), not a human gate.
readjudication_2026_09_26.performance_flag: Not flagged and not applicable: P-266 reports a prevalence and logistic-regression odds ratios, with no AUC or accuracy.
readjudication_2026_09_26.reasoning: Demote. The prior is an inflated form, supplied by the reviewer, of a belief the corpus holds only as 'mid-life obesity is a modifiable dementia risk factor', with sleep and diet as emerging candidates. P-266 does not test even that. It is a cross-sectional community screen powered for prevalence, with a clinical ACE-III cut-off, diet measured as vegetarian vs non-vegetarian and sleep as a self-reported dichotomy. It has no obese BMI contrast, and its non-significant ORs have wide intervals. An underpowered null is neither a disproof nor a boundary condition. The non-Western framing is the reviewer's, and KA-22's own disproof signal is not met. The challenger re-found every auditor quote in a fresh PDF extract and in the manuscript. No missed attestation or evidence rescues the record.

invalidated_assumptions.assumption_type: Modality superiority — functional vs structural connectivity
invalidated_assumptions.prior_belief: The dominant assumption in functional-connectivity MCI research is that resting-state fMRI functional connectivity is the necessary and superior modality for detecting network-level disruption, with structural DTI connectivity treated as secondary.
invalidated_assumptions.what_disproved_it: In P-56 (N=64, single-center, LOOCV), structural DTI connectivity alone achieved 92.19% accuracy (AUC 0.99) versus 71.88% (AUC 0.78) for rs-fMRI functional connectivity - a ~20-point gap that contradicts, in this single cohort, the assumption that functional connectivity is the superior modality. This is a counterexample requiring replication, not a definitive field-wide refutation.
invalidated_assumptions.clinical_implication: DTI structural connectivity may be at least as discriminative as rs-fMRI for MCI detection in some cohorts; requires external replication before adoption as a first-line marker.
invalidated_assumptions.review_note: G5 moderate: directional (DTI 92% vs rs-fMRI 72%, 20pt gap) but N=64 thin and unreplicated - REQUIRES REPLICATION; not definitive. | G5 CONFIRM-with-caveat 2026-07-29 (AI-adversarial): grounding verified vs summary; overclaim softened; scope/power caveat added.
invalidated_assumptions.g5_caveat: Single small (N=64), single-center, LOOCV cross-sectional study, no external validation; AUC 0.99 on N=64 likely optimistic/overfit-prone. A directional counterexample needing replication, not a field-wide disproof.
invalidated_assumptions.prior_audit_2026_08_29: ADD_NEW_PRIOR:KA-14. Add KA-14 (fMRI-FC superiority over DTI, modality fmri) and set assumption_id=KA-14; alternatively widen KA-07's belief text to cover functional-vs-structural connectivity and map there.

invalidated_assumptions.assumption_type: Necessity of cognitive testing for screening
invalidated_assumptions.prior_belief: The standard assumption is that MCI screening requires neuropsychological assessment — at minimum an MMSE — because cognitive impairment is definitionally a cognitive phenomenon that physical examination cannot detect. Routine blood tests and physical exam variables are considered screening aids at best, not primary diagnostic tools.
invalidated_assumptions.what_disproved_it: P-96 (Random Forest on CHARLS; 7 routine physical-exam/blood variables; SHAP-topping grip strength and creatinine) screened MCI without cognitive testing, externally validated at AUROC 0.83-0.87 (CHARLS 2011 + Yiwu cohort). Note: MMSE defined the training LABELS, so cognitive testing is displaced from screening-time inference, not eliminated from the diagnostic chain.
invalidated_assumptions.clinical_implication: MCI can be screened at community scale in Chinese populations from routine physical/blood data (external validation to date is CHARLS/Yiwu only); cross-cultural generalisability is unproven and the underlying sample size is not reported in source.
invalidated_assumptions.review_note: Human G5 2026-06-26: SOLID. Externally validated AUROC 0.83-0.87, no cognitive testing. | G5 CONFIRM-with-caveat 2026-07-29 (AI-adversarial): grounding verified vs summary; overclaim softened; scope/power caveat added.

readjudication_2026_09_26.attestation: None found for the belief as held. The auditor searched summaries.md with regex passes on screening/diagnosis 'requires/relies on' cognitive or neuropsychological testing or the MMSE, on 'cannot be detected without', and on routine/EHR/claims data being insufficient. The auditor also read the P-96 and P-1422 PDFs. I re-searched summaries.md for '(without|in the absence of|before) (a|any) (cognitive test|neuropsychological|MMSE)'. Every hit is a note about a study's own limitations (case ascertainment or covariates), and none states that screening requires cognitive testing. The closest statements describe current DIAGNOSTIC PRACTICE and treat it as a limitation to overcome. P-1272 (block): 'MCI diagnosis currently relies on neuropsychological testing with few validated plasma biomarkers'. P-1400 (block): 'a condition whose diagnosis currently relies on cognitive testing alone'. P-1108 (block): 'Existing MCI detection relies on clinical assessment/neuropsychological tests that miss subtle early changes'. P-1422 (PDF p.2): 'MCI is often diagnosed by a clinician using an objective cognitive assessment such as the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE).' P-1422 also cites existing routine-data MCI risk models ('South Korean National Health Insurance ... AUC 0.67-0.75'). P-96's own framing (PDF p.2, verified) is about operations: 'These limitations render MMSE unsuitable for large-scale screening'. The 'definitionally cognitive' clause is a truism, the 'physical examination cannot detect' clause is a strawman, and the rest describes practice. NOT attested.
readjudication_2026_09_26.evidence: P-96 PDF: downloads/4. Computational Models and Modern AI Architectures/1-s2.0-S1386505625002473-main.pdf (Wu et al. 2025, Int J Med Inform 203:106030). I re-extracted it and confirmed each point. (1) The seven variables are 'education, grip strength, height, weight, creatinine, mean corpuscular volume, and platelet count'. The label is 'scoring ≽1 SD below their age group's mean MMSE' (an AACD-based criterion). (2) Section 3.5: 'education was the most influential feature, with a positive average SHAP value of 0.22'. In the local example, 'creatinine has no significant effect (0)'. (3) Section 5: 'no education-based adjustment was applied'. (4) Section 2.6: the output is a binary 'high risk (1) or low risk (0)' flag. (5) Table 3 AUROC: 0.93 (0.91-0.95) on the training set, 0.83 on External Set 1 (Yiwu 2021) and 0.87 on External Set 2 (CHARLS 2011, which may share participants with CHARLS 2015). (6) Table 2 unique N: 2,932 / 4,140 / 1,782. The MMSE still defines the labels and the output is a triage flag, which is the 'screening aid' the prior already concedes. So the study does not test the prior. Record errors: education is one of the '7 routine physical-exam/blood variables'; education, not grip strength or creatinine, topped SHAP; the record says 'screened MCI' but the target is an MMSE-defined risk flag; it says the sample size is not reported, but Table 2 gives it; and CHARLS 2011 is not a fully independent cohort.
readjudication_2026_09_26.audit_2026_08_29_assessment: Recommendation: ADD_NEW_PRIOR:KA-16. The reason does not hold. KA-16 was derived from IA-31 itself (its provenance reads 'Corpus prior implied by the invalidated-assumption records listed in currently_invalidated_by'), so it is a prior supplied by the reviewer, which the H.1 independence rule excludes. No corpus study states it. Its 'no usable screening signal' clause is contradicted by the EHR, claims and risk-factor models in the corpus (P-1422 and the work it cites; P-798). KA-16 should not be confirmed. Once IA-31 is demoted, its currently_invalidated_by list is empty.
readjudication_2026_09_26.performance_flag: Not flagged. Development AUROC is 0.93 (below 0.97) on a training N of 2,932, with two external cohorts (N 4,140 and 1,782; AUROC 0.83 and 0.87). P-96 is not in the suspect set.
readjudication_2026_09_26.reasoning: Demote. I concur after re-reading the PDF and re-searching the corpus. The prior is not attested: the corpus describes diagnostic practice as a limitation, and routine-data risk models already exist in the corpus. The evidence also does not test the prior: the labels are MMSE-defined and not adjusted for education, education is the top SHAP feature, and the output is a triage flag, which is the role the prior already grants. Five statements in the record are wrong against the PDF. I considered rescoping to 'bounded' and rejected it, because there is no attested prior to bound, and line 153 already carries the remaining finding as a study-level result. For the operator, not applied: the P-96 summaries.md block repeats these defects.

invalidated_assumptions.assumption_type: ERP biomarker pattern specificity in PD-MCI
invalidated_assumptions.prior_belief: Because MCI is defined by memory impairment and semantic memory is closely linked to episodic memory, the standard assumption is that N400 amplitude — the neural marker of semantic access difficulty — is reduced in PD-MCI during language processing, mirroring the pattern seen in amnestic MCI.
invalidated_assumptions.what_disproved_it: P-370 (N=20 PD-MCI, 58 PD-NC, 24 HC; single cross-sectional ERP cohort) found that in PD-MCI the N400 abnormality was not confined to amplitude: alongside REDUCED amplitude, PD-MCI showed markedly prolonged N400 latency (~500ms vs 400ms) and impaired congruency, while PD-NC retained a larger PNP than both groups. This indicates PD-MCI involves a qualitatively broader post-semantic integration/timing deficit rather than the amplitude-only semantic-access reduction assumed by analogy to amnestic MCI.
invalidated_assumptions.clinical_implication: PD-MCI's N400 signature includes a latency/timing component beyond amplitude, so latency-sensitive ERP measures may add value. NOTE: the earlier claim that amplitude-based screens would 'miss' PD-MCI is UNSUPPORTED - the paper found amplitude IS reduced. Requires replication in a larger, ideally longitudinal, cohort.
invalidated_assumptions.review_note: G5 moderate: latency-not-amplitude invalidation is valid; NB the screening-tool clinical_implication is REVIEWER-DERIVED, not stated by the paper. | G5 CONFIRM-with-caveat 2026-07-29 (AI-adversarial): grounding verified vs summary; overclaim softened; scope/power caveat added. | FACTUAL FIX: prior record wrongly said N400 amplitude NOT reduced; paper found amplitude IS reduced. Corrected; unsupported 'amplitude screens miss PD-MCI' implication dropped.
invalidated_assumptions.g5_caveat: FACTUAL CORRECTION: the paper found PD-MCI N400 amplitude IS reduced (plus prolonged latency + impaired congruency) - the invalidation is that the deficit is qualitatively broader (latency prolongation), NOT that amplitude is spared. Single small cross-sectional cohort (N=20 PD-MCI); PD-MCI != amnestic MCI.
invalidated_assumptions.prior_audit_2026_08_29: DEMOTE:the stated prior was CONFIRMED, not disproved - P-370 found N400 amplitude IS reduced in PD-MCI; the extra latency finding is an extension. Demote to 'proposed' or reclassify as a complementary finding to IA-28/KA-21; correct the P-370 sample-size field to '102 - 20 PD-MCI/58 PD-NC/24 HC'.

readjudication_2026_09_26.reader: assistant (a language model), under the operator's delegation of 2026-09-26: one auditor and one challenger instructed to refute it, each reading the source PDF and searching the corpus for the prior; the verdict was applied without a human re-reading, so it is not a gate
readjudication_2026_09_26.attestation: Not attested in the form written. No corpus study says that N400 amplitude should be reduced in PD-MCI, and none says so by analogy with amnestic MCI 'because MCI is defined by memory impairment'. That sentence was supplied by the reviewer: KA-41 was registered from this record itself by the 2026-09-09 triage and is still status proposed_2026_09_09. Search: summaries.md for N400 (hits only in P-28, P-362, P-370 and P-658) and for PD-MCI or Parkinson plus ERP, N400, language or semantic (hits only in P-370 and P-397, an event-related-oscillation study with no N400). The nearest attested belief is about MCI on the AD spectrum, not PD-MCI. P-658 block, Best Metric: 'N400 amplitude differentiated AD from HC in 76 % of studies and MCI from HC in 67 %'. P-362 block: 'ERP findings: No significant group differences in N400 or LPC amplitudes (contrary to expectation).' The P-370 PDF itself states a different hypothesis, about PD patients against controls: 'compared to controls, the magnitude of the effect or its onset latency might be delayed, reflecting more difficult or slower semantic processing compared to controls' (pp. 113-114), and for between-group comparisons says 'we did not have a priori hypotheses of the direction of the effects in this case'. It mentions amnestic MCI only in its conclusion: 'altered N400 effects are associated with a higher risk of transiting to dementia in individuals with amnesic MCI (Olichney et al., 2008)'.
readjudication_2026_09_26.evidence:
PDF: downloads/5. Neuroimaging and Neurophysiological Biomarkers/1-s2.0-S0010945221001507-main.pdf (Leon-Cabrera et al. 2021, Cortex 141:112-127; extract at scratchpad/r15/ia/a16aud_P-370.txt).
(1) The PD-MCI group was compared with a matched PD subsample, never with controls: 'a subsample of Parkinson's disease patients with normal cognition (sPD-NC) (N=19) with an age-, gender-, education- and years of disease evolution-matched PD patients with mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI) (N=20)' (s2.3).
(2) Amplitude and onset were as expected in PD-MCI: 'Compared to a matched subgroup of PD patients with normal cognition, PD patients with MCI also exhibited expected N400 amplitude modulations within the normal onset latency (i.e., about 300-400 msec post-word onset). However, most remarkably, PD patients with MCI showed a significantly prolonged N400 congruency effect in predictive contexts, extending up to 700 msec after word onset.' (s4.2)
(3) Constraint effect: significant for both PD-NC and PD-MCI (p<.001), 'No differences between groups were found.' (s3.1.2)
(4) The congruency effect was present in PD-MCI (p=.001), not impaired. Group difference: 'a significant cluster (p=.008) that revealed a longer-lasting effect of congruency for the group of patients with MCI ... the cluster spanned approximately from 630 to 760 msec after word onset at centro-parietal sites' (s3.1.2).
(5) PNP: no group differences for controls vs PD-NC nor for sPD-NC vs PD-MCI; authors cite 'insufficient statistical power to detect differences, as sample size was smaller in this case' (s4.2).
(6) Correlations in all 78 PD patients: PNP with verbal fluency r(77)=.326, pHB=.010; prolonged congruency effect 'correlates with worse mean verbal fluency scores (r(78)=-.358, pHB=.005)'.
(7) Method: EEG 'recorded from 19 electrodes'; word-by-word presentation (300 msec per word, 200 msec blank); 312 sentences in two lists of 156. Sample: PD-NC N=58, Control N=24, PD-MCI N=20.
The record's what_disproved_it is wrong against this PDF on four points: 'REDUCED amplitude' (PDF: expected amplitude modulations); 'markedly prolonged N400 latency (~500ms vs 400ms)' (onset latency normal; what was prolonged was the duration of the congruency effect); 'impaired congruency' (congruency effect significant in PD-MCI, p=.001); 'PD-NC retained a larger PNP than both groups' (no PNP group difference in either comparison). The summary block's figures (~500 vs 400 ms, r=-0.38 p=.004, r=-0.45 p=.02, 64-channel Neuroscan, self-paced reading, 200 sentences at 80/20, sample size 24, its 'Full title') are absent from the PDF. The block is a defective, largely invented record.
readjudication_2026_09_26.audit_2026_08_29_assessment: The audit recommended DEMOTE (to 'proposed' or reclassify as a complementary finding to IA-28/KA-21) and correcting the P-370 sample size to '102 - 20 PD-MCI/58 PD-NC/24 HC'. The conclusion is right but the stated reason is wrong: its premise, 'P-370 found N400 amplitude IS reduced in PD-MCI', came from the defective summary block; the PDF reports 'expected N400 amplitude modulations within the normal onset latency'. Demotion holds for other reasons: (a) what_disproved_it contradicts the source on four points, so the anchor does not reconcile; (b) the prior is not attested in the corpus; (c) the source's actual findings cannot test an amplitude prior (a 20 vs 19 no-difference result against a PD comparator, no PD-MCI vs healthy-control contrast; the one positive finding extends rather than overturns). Reclassification as a CF with IA-28 is not supported: IA-28 is demoted (A06) and two nulls in different populations cannot jointly support an insight. The sample-size correction is right: 58 + 20 + 24 = 102 (the 19 sPD-NC lie within the 58). The block's '24', copied into registry Sample_N_Approx and logs/appraisal_worksheet.csv, is wrong.
readjudication_2026_09_26.performance_flag: Not flagged. P-370 is an ERP group-comparison study with no classifier. Registry Best_Metric and Best_AUC 'not reported'; P-370 is not in data/conflicts.json summary.inflated_performance_flags (22 entries). Appraisal-worksheet row: cross_sectional, V2.
readjudication_2026_09_26.reasoning: IA-32 fails every cell of the H.1 rule. Attestation: the PD-MCI amplitude prior 'by analogy with amnestic MCI' was supplied by the reviewer; no corpus study states it, and the registry entry was generated from this record. Anchor: every specific claim in what_disproved_it (reduced amplitude, ~500 vs 400 ms latency, impaired congruency, larger PNP in PD-NC) contradicts the PDF; they come from a summary block whose methods, results, statistics, sample size and title do not match the paper. Test: the PDF shows normal N400 amplitude modulations and onset plus a longer-lasting congruency effect (cluster ~630-760 ms) in 20 PD-MCI vs 19 matched PD-NC; the 'normal amplitude' part is a small-sample null against a PD comparator, which cannot disprove an amplitude prior, and the positive part extends rather than overturns. The master's Section 7 wording is faithful to the PDF but has no admissible assumption behind it. Data follow-ups: re-summarise P-370 from its PDF (block defective, P-369 class); set registry and appraisal-worksheet Sample_N_Approx for P-370 to 102 (58 PD-NC, 20 PD-MCI, 24 controls); mark KA-41 not attested. CHALLENGER (2026-09-26): re-checked against the P-370 extract; all quotes confirmed verbatim (expected amplitude modulations within normal onset latency; 630-760 msec cluster; sPD-NC N=19; PD-NC N=58; Control N=24; r(78)=-.358 pHB=.005; 19 electrodes; the controls-directed 'might be delayed' hypothesis; the Olichney sentence). The paper states it had no a priori hypotheses for between-group direction, so it cannot supply the PD-MCI amplitude prior either. No missed attestation found. Demote stands.

invalidated_assumptions.prior_belief: The assumption underlying digital cognitive intervention programmes for MCI is that training one cognitive domain (e.g., memory training) produces generalised improvement across untrained domains (executive function, processing speed, attention). This generalisation claim is central to the clinical rationale for recommending cognitive training to MCI patients.
invalidated_assumptions.what_disproved_it: P-253 conducted a meta-analysis of 25–30 RCTs (2,000+ participants) of digital cognitive interventions in MCI. The finding for computerised cognitive training was effect size 0.35–0.45 on trained domains but limited transfer to untrained domains. The generalisation assumption was directly contradicted by the data — domain-specific gains did not propagate across cognitive functions. Mobile apps and telehealth showed the smallest effect sizes (SMD 0.2–0.3) despite being the most accessible modality.
invalidated_assumptions.clinical_implication: REJECTED - the underlying transfer finding does not exist in the source paper.
invalidated_assumptions.review_note: Human G5 2026-06-26 REJECTED against authoritative source (He C et al., Ageing Res Rev 2025; PMID 41271116; DOI 10.1016/j.arr.2025.102951). The record's entire evidentiary basis is FABRICATED in our summary, not present in the paper: (1) actual study count is 21 RCTs from 3414 screened, NOT '25-30'; (2) the paper reports a SINGLE pooled estimate, SMD 0.52 (95% CI 0.36-0.68) for GLOBAL cognitive function - the per-modality effect sizes (computerized 0.35-0.45, games 0.4, VR 0.45-0.6, apps/telehealth 0.2-0.3, multimodal 0.5-0.6) in our summary do not exist in the source; (3) there is NO trained-vs-untrained transfer analysis in the paper - global cognition was the outcome, so the 'limited transfer to untrained domains' claim that this entire IA rests on is unsupported. NOTE: summaries.md Paper 253 block itself contains the fabricated numbers and must be corrected; registry Sample_N_Approx ('25-30 studies') and primary_metric_type ('AUC_ROC') are also wrong (should be 21 RCTs / SMD). A DIFFERENT, properly-sourced invalidation could potentially be built on the paper's narrative success-factor #2 ('Multiple cognitive domains coverage'), but that is not what this record claims and would need its own G5 pass.
invalidated_assumptions.data_integrity_flag: summaries.md Paper 253 contains fabricated quantitative breakdowns; registry N and metric_type wrong

invalidated_assumptions.prior_belief: Multi-ingredient/multivitamin supplementation is more effective than single nutrients (e.g. omega-3) for preventing MCI, as concluded from the NMA intervention ranking in P-151.
invalidated_assumptions.what_disproved_it: The NMA ranking does not robustly support multi-ingredient superiority over omega-3: the significant Multi arm rests on N=483 vs the null Omega-3 arm's N=2293 with an implausible ~2-SD effect (small-study/precision-asymmetry pattern). This undercuts the reliability of the ranking; it does not by itself establish omega-3 superiority or multi-ingredient ineffectiveness.
invalidated_assumptions.evidence_from_summary: P-151 is an NMA of 52 trials / 8452 participants concluding the multi-ingredient intervention outperforms others (SMD 2.03, 95% CI 0.97-3.09). Per-arm sample sizes are highly imbalanced (operator-verified from the P-151 forest plot: Multi N=483 vs Omega-3 N=2293); the significant winning arm rests on far fewer participants than the null omega-3 arm.
invalidated_assumptions.clinical_implication: Comparative supplement rankings from this single NMA should be treated cautiously; the multi-ingredient>single-nutrient superiority is not robustly supported, pending better-powered head-to-head trials.
invalidated_assumptions.review_note: Human G5: confirmed; small-N-significant-over-large-N-null ranking is statistically fragile. 2026-06-30 NUMBER CORRECTION (operator-supplied from the P-151 forest plot): Multi SMD 2.03 (0.97-3.09) N=483 vs Omega-3 SMD 0.39 (-0.42-1.19) N=2293. The original record's figures (Multi 3.58/N=129; Omega-3 0.63/N=773) were incorrect and have been replaced. Fragility conclusion unchanged and arguably strengthened: the significant winner rests on ~4.4x fewer participants than the null omega-3 arm and reports an implausibly large ~2-SD effect. | G5 CONFIRM-with-caveat 2026-07-29 (AI-adversarial): grounding verified vs summary; overclaim softened; scope/power caveat added.
invalidated_assumptions.g5_caveat: Statistical-reliability critique of one NMA's ranking, not an external empirical refutation. Shows the ranking is not robust (significant Multi arm N=483 above null Omega-3 arm N=2293); does NOT establish omega-3 superiority or multi-ingredient ineffectiveness.
invalidated_assumptions.prior_audit_2026_08_29: DEMOTE:single-paper statistical critique of one NMA ranking, not a field prior; per-arm Ns are not in the summary block. Demote to 'proposed' (or move to a quality-flag note on P-151 in the registry Primary_Limitation); the summary block also needs its raw-abstract Key-findings text replaced.

readjudication_2026_09_26.reader: assistant (a language model), under the operator's delegation of 2026-09-26: one auditor and one challenger instructed to refute it, each reading the source PDF and searching the corpus for the prior; the verdict was applied without a human re-reading, so it is not a gate
readjudication_2026_09_26.attestation: None found as a belief held in the field and stated independently of the study that is supposed to disprove it. The prior is written as P-151's own conclusion ('as concluded from the NMA intervention ranking in P-151'). The P-151 abstract says: 'Our NMA amalgamated evidence underscoring multi-ingredient interventions as the most efficacious strategy for attenuating cognitive decline in individuals with MCI and AD.' The only other statements close to the prior are inside P-151's own discussion: 'reviews and meta-analyses yielded either no evidence or insufficient evidence to support the benefits of single nutrients [24,87-90]', and 'Epidemiological studies have indicated that the consumption of moderate doses of antioxidant vitamins, akin to those found in multivitamin supplements, may be linked to a ...'. These are citations inside the same study. They support its conclusion; they are not an independent statement of a belief that something else in the corpus overturns. I accept the auditor's searches (multi-nutrient, Souvenaid, Fortasyn, single nutrient, multi-ingredient, multivitamin). P-881 (a single-nutrient versus dietary-pattern rationale in observational type 2 diabetes work), P-1405 (a drafter's comparison) and P-860 (credits prior results to multi-ingredient formulations) do not state the prior. The record also says 'for preventing MCI', but P-151 enrols people who already have MCI or AD.
readjudication_2026_09_26.evidence: PDF downloads/4. Computational Models and Modern AI Architectures/1-s2.0-S2405457725001317-main.pdf (He et al. 2025, Clin Nutr ESPEN 67:555-566). I re-extracted it and checked every figure. Abstract: 'the multi-ingredient intervention outperformed other interventions significantly (SMD = 2.03; 95% CrI = 0.97-3.09, P = 0.0002)'. s3.1: '6 studies (483 participants) examined the effect of Multi ... 10 studies (2293 participants) examined the effect of changes in levels of omega-3'. Fig. 2C: 'Omega-3 0.39 (-0.42, 1.19)'. s3.3: 'The P-values of node-splitting analysis between the direct and indirect effects of Multi and omega-3 were <0.05'; 'The effect size of Multi was higher in the high risk of bias studies (SMD = 2.20, 95%CrI = 0.42-4.00, P = 0.004'; 'Multi ranked the second with SUCRA value of 0.79 in MCI subgroup (SMD = 1.22, 95%CrI = 0.75-1.68'. Fig. 4 (MCI subgroup, 26 trials, sample size 4,759): 'CH 3.52 (2.98, 4.06)', 'Multi 1.22 (0.75, 1.68)', 'Omega-3 0.02 (-0.04, 0.07)', 'I2 = 44.2%'. s3.4: 'SMD = 0.71, 95%CrI = 0.27-1.15 ... overall I2 value of 80 %. We did not find evidence of a superior effect of other nutritional interventions'. Discussion: 'it is important to exercise caution when interpreting these results due to the presence of inconsistency among the included studies.' Limitations: 'the number of studies (n = 6) included in our NMA, which investigated multi-ingredient intervention, was limited.' The methods name funnel plots and Egger's test, but the text reports no result for either. Assessment: P-151 supports the prior rather than disproving it. The 'bound' is a reviewer's reading of a fragility that the authors flag themselves, and the record's 'small-study/precision-asymmetry pattern' was never tested in the source. One caveat: the sample-size column of Fig. 2C comes out scrambled in extraction and may print a different Multi total from the 483 in the text. The text value is used.
readjudication_2026_09_26.audit_2026_08_29_assessment: Recommendation: 'DEMOTE: single-paper statistical critique of one NMA ranking, not a field prior; per-arm Ns are not in the summary block ...'. The main reason holds: the prior is P-151's own conclusion, and the critique is a quality flag. The subsidiary reasons are out of date. The block was rewritten from the PDF on 2026-09-15 and now carries the per-arm Ns, and the Primary_Limitation quality flag is already recorded in the registry and the block. The 2026-09-19 human admit (worksheet item 36) judged whether the facts are supported, which they are. It did not test whether the prior is independent of the study, and that test fails.
readjudication_2026_09_26.performance_flag: Not applicable and not flagged. P-151 is a network meta-analysis of 52 double-blind RCTs (8,452 participants) with no classifier. Its registry Best_Metric is an SMD with no Acc/AUC/F1 tag.
readjudication_2026_09_26.reasoning: The challenger confirms the auditor's demote, and every quoted figure is in the re-extracted PDF. The prior fails independence: it is P-151's own conclusion, so the same study both holds the belief and 'disproves' it, and the disproof is a reviewer's statistical reading, which is a quality flag. The evidence also points the wrong way for a disproof, because P-151 supports multi-ingredient benefit and discloses its own fragility. The record misstates the population ('preventing MCI') and claims a small-study asymmetry that the source never tested. One factual correction to the auditor: in the MCI subgroup, multi-ingredient is not the only node above placebo. Chinese herbal (SMD 3.52, 2.98-4.06) ranks first. Computational Models and Modern AI Architectures/PMID_35455005_life-12-00514.pdf): "97 images of AD, 293 images of MCI patient and 192 images of cognitive normal"; "To differentiate MCI and CN, both V-model and R-model achieved excellent performance, with an AUC of 0.9992 [+/-] 0.0022"; "the ten-fold cross validation was adopted for model training and validation. The second dataset has "35 Control subjects (CO), 31 Mild AD patients, and 22 Moderate AD patients", so no MCI group, and "The classification and reporting of accuracy were based on the same experimental setting as the first dataset". P-197 (downloads/4. .../PMID_35161486_sensors-22-00740.pdf): "25 subjects were used from each of the five categories of AD, MCI, EMCI, LMCI, and NC (a total of 125 subjects)". P-1 (downloads/4. .../1-s2.0-S001048252200909X-main.pdf): "ensemble model was effective (98.81% accuracy) at EMCI to AD conversion prediction"; ADNI (383), internal cross-validation. invalidated_assumptions.prior_belief: Whole-image deep learning extracts richer prognostic information than simple interpretable region-based or clinical models, and therefore improves MCI-to-dementia conversion prediction.
invalidated_assumptions.what_disproved_it: P-274 (Arvidsson 2024; BioFINDER-1 SCD/MCI n=332 under double cross-validation, external ADNI MCI n=108) compared a 3D CNN on whole-brain MRI and Jacobian-determinant images plus clinical data with clinical-data, clinical-plus-hippocampal-volume and clinical-plus-FreeSurfer-regions models. For four-year progression to AD dementia the DL model (test AUC 0.84) did not differ significantly from the clinical-data model (0.85) and was significantly worse than the clinical-plus-hippocampal-volume model (0.86; Mann-Whitney U over cross-validation folds, p < 0.05); for four-year MMSE slope every other model was significantly better than DL (R2 0.08 vs 0.14-0.17). On external ADNI data the DL model's AUC fell to 0.80, significantly below its BioFINDER-1 result.
invalidated_assumptions.evidence_from_summary: P-274 (PMID 38504336): clinical AUC 0.85/R2 0.14; clinical+hippocampal AUC 0.86; clinical+regional AUC 0.83/R2 0.17; DL AUC 0.84/R2 0.08, explicitly 'worse than simpler region-based baselines'. N=332 + external ADNI n=108.
invalidated_assumptions.clinical_implication: In patients with SCD or MCI, at a training size of a few hundred and with a deliberately parameter-efficient 3D CNN, whole-image DL did not improve conversion or cognitive-decline prediction over clinical data plus hippocampal volume, so simple interpretable models remain the benchmark at this scale. The authors attribute the result to limited data and model capacity and caution that DL may need an order of magnitude more data, so the finding bounds rather than refutes the prior (one study; mixed SCD/MCI development cohort).
invalidated_assumptions.review_note: G5: Excellent. Prospectively designed with EXTERNAL ADNI validation (not post-hoc); DL loses to clinical model on both AUC and R2. | G5 CONFIRM-with-caveat 2026-07-29 (AI-adversarial): grounding verified vs summary; overclaim softened; scope/power caveat added.
invalidated_assumptions.g5_caveat: One prospective study on a MIXED SCD/MCI cohort (not pure MCI). AUC difference is small with no significance test/CIs (best read 'did not outperform'); the stronger signal is degraded MMSE-slope R2. Scope to this task/cohort family, not a universal DL refutation.
invalidated_assumptions.prior_audit_2026_08_29: ADD_NEW_PRIOR:KA-15. Add KA-15 (complexity-extracts-more-information) and set assumption_id=KA-15.

second_reader_2026_09_15.note: P-274's block (title: "Comparing a pre-defined versus deep learning approach for extracting brain atrophy patterns...", Arvidsson 2024, matches the cited PMID) reports a within-study null exactly as the record states: "Clinical model: AUC 0.85... R2 0.14", "Clinical + hippocampal volume: AUC 0.86; R2 0.16", "Clinical + regional MRI volumes: AUC 0.83; R2 0.17", "DL model: AUC 0.84; R2 0.08 (worse than simpler region-based baselines)", with "BioFINDER-1 SCD/MCI participants (n=332)" and "ADNI subset (n=108)" as external cohort. The prior is a genuine field assumption the paper itself set out to test ("Many studies assume deep imaging models are superior; this work directly and rigorously tests that assumption"), and the record's clinical_implication already bounds the finding to SCD/MCI on this single cohort family; the only clause not literally in the block is the hedge "not significance-tested", which weakens rather than inflates the claim.

readjudication_2026_09_26.attestation: P-37 (Bae et al. 2021, Neurobiology of Aging; PDF downloads/4. Computational Models and Modern AI Architectures/1-s2.0-S0197458020304140-main.pdf, Introduction; the challenger re-extracted it and found the text verbatim): "previous research has relied on specific features (e.g., cortical thickness and hippocampal volume) extracted from raw data to train the model (Zheng and Casari, 2018). This approach assumes that the chosen feature is the most informative and may neglect important information inherent in the raw data. CNN is a deep-learning approach that has evolved in recent years to produce better classification performance and feature visualization than conventional machine learning methods across several fields (Borji et al., 2019). A CNN trained on raw, whole brain data can automatically extract the important imaging features and can offer insights beyond current methods in predicting disease progression." This is a belief held in the field (cited to Borji 2019), not P-274's own hypothesis. Supporting, from P-274's own Discussion (verbatim): "in the study by [22], they received significantly better results using a DL model and MRI images compared to e.g. MMSE, hippocampal volume, cerebrospinal fluid Aβ and tau". The block phrase "Many studies assume deep imaging models are superior", quoted by the 2026-09-15 second reader, was written by the summariser and does not appear in the P-274 PDF. Attestation therefore rests on P-37.
readjudication_2026_09_26.evidence: PDF downloads/4. Computational Models and Modern AI Architectures/PMID_38504336_13195_2024_Article_1428.pdf (Arvidsson et al. 2024), all re-extracted by the challenger. Methods: "the results from the 10 folds were used in a Mann-Whitney U-test ... All p-values less than 0.05 were considered significant. Bootstrapping on the test sets was used to estimate 95% confidence". Results: clinical model "mean BioFINDER test AUC of 0.850 (CI 0.698-0.954)"; "Adding whole brain MRI and JD images to the clinical data together in a CNN model led to a decreased test AUC of 0.840 (CI 0.688-0.957)"; "it was found that the hippocampal volume model was significantly better (p-value < 0.05) than both the FreeSurfer and DL models, the Clinical data model was significantly better than the FreeSurfer model, while there was no significant difference between any other pair of models. The results for the external ADNI test data had no significant difference in performance from the BioFINDER test data except for the FreeSurfer model and DL model, which performed significantly worse (FreeSurfer: AUC 0.688, CI 0.536-0.827, DL: AUC 0.799, CI 0.677-0.904)". MMSE slope R2: clinical 0.138, clinical plus hippocampal volume 0.157, clinical plus FreeSurfer regions 0.175; "The DL model ... had the lowest mean test R2 of 0.079 (-0.206-0.267) ... All models were significantly better (p-value < 0.05) than the DL model". Cohort: "for this study the SCD and MCI groups were analyzed together". The authors' own limit: "the results should not be interpreted as a failure for DL, but rather that its success might require an order of magnitude more data" and "the worse performance of the DL model is probably caused by its limited capacity, chosen to fit the number of subjects available". The study tests the prior head to head: same participants, same protocol, plus an external cohort. The PDF contradicts two phrases in the record: 'not significance-tested' in what_disproved_it and 'no significance test/CIs' in g5_caveat.

Registering a prior does not attest it. P-37 supplies the independent corpus attestation that Appendix H.1 requires, and KA-15's assumed_since and provenance should cite it before the prior is confirmed. The audit did not recommend demotion and none is warranted.
readjudication_2026_09_26.performance_flag: Not flagged. BioFINDER-1 test AUCs were 0.832 to 0.862 (DL 0.840) under double cross-validation, and there is an external ADNI cohort of n=108 (DL AUC 0.799, best model 0.86). This is below the 0.97 threshold and externally validated.
readjudication_2026_09_26.reasoning: The challenger re-extracted P-37 and P-274 and found every auditor quote verbatim. The prior is attested independently by P-37's introduction, which states it as a field belief cited to Borji 2019, and by P-274's discussion of an earlier study that found DL significantly better. P-274 tests the prior directly, on the same data and protocol with an external cohort, and it is not performance-flagged. It reports Mann-Whitney tests and bootstrap CIs, so the record's 'not significance-tested' is false and the record cannot be kept as written. The evidence is one study of 332 people, and the authors explicitly attribute the result to data size and model capacity, so the classification is bounded, not refuted. invalidated_assumptions.prior_belief: Machine-learning survival models (Random Survival Forest, XGBoost) outperform classical Cox proportional-hazards regression for predicting MCI-to-AD progression.
invalidated_assumptions.what_disproved_it: P-309 (Guan 2025; NACC UDS 3.0, n=3,674 MCI, one 7:3 train/validation split, no external validation, median follow-up 24.5 months) fitted Random Survival Forest, XGBoost and Cox models to the same 13 clinical, neuropsychological, demographic and APOE predictors (selected by RSF/XGBoost importance and SHAP; no imaging): validation C-index 0.781 (RSF), 0.781 (XGBoost) and 0.797 (Cox; 0.798 without APOE e4), and the authors conclude the ML models were 'not better than' Cox. No confidence interval or significance test is reported for the differences, and the ML models fell from training C-index 0.861/0.840 to 0.781 on validation.
invalidated_assumptions.evidence_from_summary: P-147 (J Prev Alzheimers Dis 2025, 1-s2.0-S2274580725000275): NACC n=3674 MCI subjects; RSF/XGBoost/Cox compared by C-index; summary states 'the prediction effects of the XGBoost and RSF models were not better than those of the Cox model.'
invalidated_assumptions.clinical_implication: In a large NACC MCI cohort with low-dimensional clinical predictors, ML survival models gave no advantage over Cox, so Cox is a competitive, interpretable baseline there. The ordering is not general: on ADNI with imaging predictors the random survival forest significantly exceeded Cox (C-index 0.878 vs 0.863; P-344) while gradient boosting trailed it, so ML survival models should be benchmarked against Cox on the target cohort before adoption.
invalidated_assumptions.review_note: G5: Excellent. Large N=3674, fair well-powered concordance comparison; independent corroboration of IA-15.
invalidated_assumptions.g5_caveat: 2026-08-15 (operator, via C-232): the model ordering this record rests on (Cox >= RSF/XGBoost, NACC UDS 3.0 n=3,674) does not replicate in ADNI - P-344 (n=902 MCI, five survival learners) reports RSF best (C-index 0.878 vs CoxPH 0.863), the reverse ordering for random survival forests only; gradient boosting trails Cox there too (GBSA 0.803), which corroborates this record. C-232 was reclassified as documented incommensurability on 2026-09-24 (different predictor sets and horizons). Also note the NACC basis is a single publication counted once: P-147 and P-309 are the same paper (registry duplicate_of set).
invalidated_assumptions.prior_audit_2026_08_29: ADD_NEW_PRIOR:KA-15. Set assumption_id=KA-15; keep the C-232 conflict pointer in g5_caveat.

The challenger confirmed that its extracted text is byte-identical to that of P-147's file, 1-s2.0-S2274580725000275-main.pdf. Abstract: "A total of 3674 subjects with MCI were included. Thirteen predictors were ultimately identified. In the validation set, the concordance indices were 0.781 (RSF), 0.781 (XGBoost), and 0.798 (Cox), and the Integrated Brier Score was 0.087 (Cox). invalidated_assumptions.prior_belief: Published MCI machine-learning models that report high in-study performance (AUC>0.80, accuracy>70%) reflect diagnostic/prognostic ability that will generalise to real-world, non-ADNI populations.
invalidated_assumptions.what_disproved_it: P-329, a systematic review of 138 MCI ML studies, found that while more than half report AUC>0.8 and accuracy>70%, about TWO-THIRDS rely on ADNI and only ~10% perform any external validation. In-study performance is 'often good' but external testing is 'uncommon'; the review explicitly attributes this to overfitting to benchmark cohorts and weak out-of-sample testing. High in-study accuracy therefore does not establish generalisable performance.
invalidated_assumptions.evidence_from_summary: P-329 (PMID 40567069, systematic review, 138 studies): >half AUC>0.8 & acc>70%; ~2/3 ADNI-only; only ~10% externally validated; review flags ADNI-dependence, small samples, inconsistent external testing as generalizability risks.
invalidated_assumptions.clinical_implication: Reported MCI ML accuracies should be treated as optimistic until externally validated; deployment claims require non-ADNI (ideally prospective) validation. Systematically corroborates IA-14 (suspect >98% accuracies) and gap ACTOR-G-010 (no standardized benchmark).
invalidated_assumptions.actor_note: STRONG: systematic review (n=138 studies) quantifying field-level external-validation failure.

invalidated_assumptions.prior_audit_2026_08_29: DEMOTE:evidence shows generalisation is rarely tested, not that it fails; meta-level methodological claim rather than a domain prior. readjudication_2026_09_26.attestation: None found. KA-36 is status proposed_2026_09_09 and was registered from the IA record itself ("from confirmed IA records that named no registered prior"). The corpus attests a practice, internal-only validation, which P-329 documents. It does not attest a stated belief that in-study performance generalises. P-329 expresses promise only: "Multimodal prediction models for Alzheimer's disease (AD) are emerging as promising tools for improving detection and informing prognosis" and "have great potential to be used to assist clinical decision-making". Individual papers claim that their own model generalises (e.g., P-119), but those are per-paper claims, not a field prior. The challenger's second search (assumption/belief phrasing, over-optimism, leakage, external-validation drops) found nothing further. Read literally, the prior is a strawman that contradicts standard prediction-model methodology.
readjudication_2026_09_26.evidence: P-329 (downloads/4. Computational Models and Modern AI Architectures/PMID_40567069_10.1177_13872877251351630.pdf) is a scoping review, not a systematic review of MCI ML studies: "The literature review was conducted following the Arksey and O'Malley framework for scoping reviews". It covers 138 multimodal AD-spectrum prediction-model studies ("N=89; 64.5%" MCI-to-AD). "More than half of the prediction models reported an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve exceeding 0.8 and an accuracy exceeding 70%. However, 66.7% of the prediction models were developed using data from the ADNI study, and only 10.1% of the models went through external validation". "findings from existing literature may not generalize to populations outside of ADNI participants". "incorporating elements closely related to the outcomes of interest as main predictors and training models on small datasets may have inflated model performance" (the PDF text prints this as 'in fl ated'). The one direct test, which the record omits: "eight out of eleven studies reported a lower AUC in external validation datasets compared to development datasets ... The accuracy was lower in the external validation datasets than in the development datasets in half of the six studies that reported accuracy." That is a direction count with no magnitudes and no quality appraisal ("the studies included in the literature review did not go through quality assessments"). The record misstates the source: it calls the paper a "systematic review of 138 MCI ML studies"; the words 'often good' and 'uncommon' are absent from the PDF (they come from the summary block's paraphrase); and 'overfitting to benchmark cohorts and weak out-of-sample testing' is not in the PDF either (it is summariser commentary, misattributed).
readjudication_2026_09_26.audit_2026_08_29_assessment: The recommendation was DEMOTE, and its reason holds: the evidence shows that generalisation is rarely tested (about 10%), not that it fails, and the claim is methodological rather than a domain prior. One correction: P-329 does contain a direct comparison (8 of 11 lower AUC; 3 of 6 lower accuracy). With no magnitudes, it could bound only a truism, so it cannot rescue an unattested prior. The advice to cite P-329 as a caution is already followed in master Section 3.4, accurately. Do not house IA-14 and IA-17 under one KA.
readjudication_2026_09_26.performance_flag: Not flagged. P-329 is a scoping review with no performance metric of its own (Best_Metric 'not reported', T6).
readjudication_2026_09_26.reasoning: The prior is unattested: it was registered from this record, and the corpus shows only a practice, not a stated belief. The anchor shows that external validation is rare, not that in-study performance fails to generalise, so it does not test the prior as written. The record also fails anchor reconciliation: wrong design, invented quotes, and summariser commentary attributed to the review. A bounded rescope ('external performance is no lower than development performance') was considered and rejected. That prior is also unattested, and the 8/11 and 3/6 direction counts have no magnitudes. The substantive point survives through the manuscript's direct, accurate citation of P-329 in Section 3.4.

invalidated_assumptions.prior_belief: Cognitive deficits observed in MCI track core AD CSF pathology (amyloid/tau), so cognitive-test abnormalities should correlate with CSF biomarkers.
invalidated_assumptions.what_disproved_it: P-386 (retrospective, N=166 MCI) found Reading-the-Mind-in-the-Eyes-Test (RMET, social cognition) correlated with structural MRI, FDG-PET, and neuropsychological measures but showed NO significant correlation with CSF biomarkers - DEMONSTRATING A DISSOCIATION that QUALIFIES (does not overturn) the assumption that MCI cognitive deficits track CSF amyloid/tau. A boundary case: CSF-normal patients can still have clinically relevant social-cognition impairment.
invalidated_assumptions.evidence_from_summary: P-386 (N=166 MCI, retrospective): RMET correlated with MRI / FDG-PET / neuropsychological measures but 'no significant correlation with CSF biomarkers.'
invalidated_assumptions.clinical_implication: CSF-biomarker normality does not exclude clinically relevant cognitive (social-cognition) impairment in MCI; multi-domain cognitive assessment captures pathology not mirrored by CSF. (MODERATE strength - single retrospective cohort; the paper itself notes compatibility with prior social-cognition literature, so 'challenges' not 'disproves'.)
invalidated_assumptions.actor_note: MODERATE: real null but expected-ish; single retrospective cohort N=166.
invalidated_assumptions.review_note: G5: weakest of the set - reframed from invalidation to DISSOCIATION / boundary condition. A single retrospective N=166 study on one cognitive domain does not overturn the amyloid/tau cascade; it usefully shows CSF-normal != cognitively-intact. | G5 CONFIRM-with-caveat 2026-07-29 (AI-adversarial): grounding verified vs summary; overclaim softened; scope/power caveat added.
invalidated_assumptions.g5_caveat: Bounded DISSOCIATION, not an invalidation: single retrospective cross-sectional correlation-only cohort (N=166) testing ONE peripheral domain (RMET social cognition); the qualitative CSF null qualifies but does not overturn amyloid/tau cognitive-tracking, and the null is arguably expected given social cognition's dissociability.
invalidated_assumptions.prior_audit_2026_08_29: DEMOTE:record itself reframes it as a 'bounded DISSOCIATION, not an invalidation'; one social-cognition test in one retrospective cohort. readjudication_2026_09_26.attestation: The prior as the record words it (KA-37: 'cognitive-test abnormalities should correlate with CSF biomarkers') is attested only as a replicated finding, and the disproving study itself reproduces that finding. P-502 (block): 'memory-related responses were shown to correlate with CSF Aβ42 and pTau181'. P-1014 (block): 'CSF Aβ was positively associated with older age and lower MMSE, and p-tau with female sex and lower MMSE'. P-730 (block): 'EMCI and LMCI were both associated with age, MMSE and CSF Abeta42'. The narrower form the evidence could at most bound is that social-cognition or emotion-recognition deficits in MCI track CSF amyloid/tau or are AD-specific. That form is NOT attested as a held belief. The closest statements are hedged proposals, and their authors acknowledge disagreement. P-949 (block, 'Why'): 'social-cognitive deficits (emotion recognition) had been proposed as early signs of AD but had never been directly compared across these patient groups'. P-386 PDF p.2: 'social cognition assessment could be valuable for differential AD diagnosis [12]. More importantly, emotion recognition could be impaired in early AD stages [13-15] even when general cognition is unimpaired, as a recent meta-analysis demonstrated [16]. However, there is some controversy in this field.' P-663 (block) calls the AD empathy literature 'sparse and contradictory'. Search method: summaries.md regexes for cognit*/neuropsycholog*/MMSE/memory within 80 characters of correlat*/associat*/track*/mirror* and CSF/cerebrospinal, in both orders (11 blocks); a second regex for social cognition/emotion recognition/theory of mind/RMET (14 blocks); P-949, P-663 and P-1129 blocks read; P-386 PDF read in full (the challenger re-extracted it).
readjudication_2026_09_26.evidence: PDF: downloads/5. Neuroimaging and Neurophysiological Biomarkers/1-s2.0-S0166432823005624-main.pdf (Gandia-Ferrero et al. 2024, Behav Brain Res 461:114844; the DOI 10.1016/j.bbr.2023.114844 matches paper_pdf_map). (1) The same study CONFIRMS the prior as worded, for the standard tests. Results p.4: 'Results showed that correlations between the standard neuropsychological evaluation (RBANS, CDR, MMSE) and CSF biomarkers levels (Aβ42, Tau, p-Tau) were statistically significant. However, RMET scores did not correlate with CSF biomarkers, although strong correlations were observed with other neuropsychological tests (see Fig. 2).' The record's what_disproved_it leaves out the first sentence, which reverses its import. (2) The RMET-CSF 'null' comes from a thresholded correlogram, not an estimate. Section 2.5 p.4: 'only simple correlations with p values ≤0.001 were reported'. Results p.4: 'results only show those correlations with a moderate or strong effect size (≥0.3)'. Any RMET-CSF correlation with |r| < 0.3 or p > 0.001 is therefore suppressed. The p-values are only in a supplementary xlsx that the corpus does not hold. (3) The cohort mixes causes by design. p.2: 'Approximately, half of these MCI cases were due to neurodegenerative diseases, showing alterations in CSF biomarkers or neuroimaging performance ... the other MCI cases did not meet the criteria for any neurodegenerative disease known (normal CSF biomarkers and neuroimaging test)'. Table 1 gives RMET total 16±5 (neurodegenerative, n=82) vs 18±5 (not neurodegenerative, n=84), with no test reported. (4) The authors did not test the dissociation. Limitations, p.7: 'further analyses would be needed to clearly depict the neuropathological trajectories of specific pathologies (e.g., MCI-AD vs MCI non-AD). However, these analyses would require larger subgroup samples.' (5) The authors' reading, p.6: 'the social cognition impairment observed in MCI was not specific for AD'. Assessment: the study does not test the record's prior, which it supports. Nor does it test the narrower social-cognition prior: the evidence there is a thresholded correlation null with no CSF-stratified comparison. The clinical_implication ('CSF-biomarker normality does not exclude clinically relevant cognitive (social-cognition) impairment') holds by cohort construction, because about half of the MCI sample had normal CSF by inclusion and no RMET comparison by CSF status is reported. It is not a finding. (6) Challenger addition, PDF p.4 Section 2.5: correlation coefficients 'between 0 and 0.3 were set to 0 (small/no correlation)' in the categorised correlograms. The RMET-CSF 'no correlation' therefore means |r| < 0.3 or p > 0.001, not r = 0.
readjudication_2026_09_26.audit_2026_08_29_assessment: The DEMOTE recommendation is right, but its stated reason is incomplete. 'Bounded, not an invalidation' is not by itself grounds to demote, because Appendix H.1 admits bounded records. 'One test, one cohort' is a strength caveat. The decisive reasons are in the PDF: (a) the same study found RBANS, CDR and MMSE significantly correlated with CSF Aβ42/Tau/p-Tau, so it supports the prior as written rather than bounding it; (b) the RMET null is an artefact of the p ≤ 0.001 and |r| ≥ 0.3 correlogram threshold, not a tested dissociation; (c) a prior specific to social cognition is not attested. The suggested fallback, listing P-386 as a weak supporter under KA-17, should NOT be taken. KA-17's disproof signal requires markers 'carrying prognostic signal in amyloid-negative MCI', and P-386 is cross-sectional with no amyloid-stratified or prognostic analysis. KA-17's two linked records (IA-03, IA-41) were also demoted in batch A04 of this round.
readjudication_2026_09_26.performance_flag: Not flagged. It is a correlational study: no classifier, and no AUC or accuracy reported (Spearman correlations; RMET vs imaging |r| 0.30-0.40). N=166 (PET n=124, MR n=85), single-centre, retrospective, no external cohort. The demotion does not rest on the flag.
readjudication_2026_09_26.reasoning: Demote. The record's prior (MCI cognitive-test abnormalities correlate with CSF amyloid/tau) is not overturned or bounded by P-386. The PDF reports significant correlations between RBANS, CDR, MMSE and CSF Aβ42, Tau and p-Tau, which confirms the prior for standard cognition, and the record omits this. The only surviving candidate is a narrower claim: that social cognition (RMET) tracks CSF pathology or is AD-specific. That claim fails twice. It is not attested as a held belief (only hedged proposals with 'some controversy'). And the evidence does not test it: the null comes from a correlogram that sets coefficients below |r| 0.3 to zero and suppresses p > 0.001, in a cohort where half the patients are non-neurodegenerative, and the MCI-AD vs non-AD comparison the dissociation needs was not run for lack of subgroup size. The clinical implication is true by construction of the cohort. Being conservative, the record does not survive, and no rescope is admissible.

invalidated_assumptions.prior_belief: In Parkinson's disease MCI (PD-MCI) specifically, amyloid PET imaging improves ML prediction of cognitive impairment over inexpensive clinical/gait features. (NB the field's amyloid-PET-helps assumption is strongest for AD-spectrum MCI, not PD-MCI.)
invalidated_assumptions.what_disproved_it: P-221 ran a direct head-to-head comparison in PD: a clinical+gait model reached >80% accuracy/specificity, while ADDING amyloid PET did NOT improve and 'often weakened' prediction. CRITICAL CAVEAT: the PET subgroup is severely underpowered (n=36: 19 PD-MCI + 17 non-PD-MCI) - this null is better read as 'insufficient power to detect a modest PET benefit' than as proven absence of incremental value.
invalidated_assumptions.evidence_from_summary: P-221 (PMID 36468069): clinical+gait Model 1 acc/spec >80%; summary: 'amyloid PET did not improve and in this study often weakened prediction.' Small cohort N=75 (PET subgroup 19 PD-MCI + 17 noPD-MCI).
invalidated_assumptions.clinical_implication: Suggestive (not conclusive) evidence that clinical/gait phenotyping may rival amyloid PET for PD-MCI screening. Present as THEMATIC SUPPORT within the 'expensive imaging != better' cluster (IA-15/16, IA-NEW-04), NOT as a standalone invalidation.
invalidated_assumptions.actor_note: MODERATE: small PET subgroup (19+17), PD-MCI-specific; paper urges sample-size caution and notes mixed prior amyloid-PET evidence.
invalidated_assumptions.review_note: G5 moderate, usable ONLY with prominent caveats: (1) PET subgroup n=36 underpowered - null != absence of effect; (2) PD-MCI pathophysiology (alpha-synuclein/dopaminergic) does NOT generalize to amnestic/AD-spectrum MCI; (3) prior_belief narrowed to PD-MCI; (4) do not present standalone.

second_reader_2026_09_15.note: P-221's block (title "Machine learning can predict mild cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease", cohort "75 PD participants (33 PD-MCI, 42 noPD-MCI)", PET subgroup "19 PD-MCI, 17 noPD-MCI") states in Outcomes that clinical+gait Model 1 reached "accuracy/specificity above 80%" and "Adding amyloid PET features reduced performance", with Key findings verbatim "amyloid PET did not improve and in this study often weakened prediction" - a within-study reversal that matches every number and quote in the record.
